title: Chapter 9: Aggregate Demand and Aggregate Supply (AD-AS)
benchmark: Paul Krugman & Robin Wells, Macroeconomics (Principles SSOT, Spring 2027)

questions.title: Aggregate Demand vs. Microeconomic Market Demand
questions.prompt_template: How does the Aggregate Demand (AD) curve fundamentally differ from a microeconomic demand curve for a single good?

hints.text: Think about what changes on the vertical axis of the AD-AS model compared to a single-market supply-and-demand diagram.
Remember that AD = C + I + G + NX relates the overall price index P to economy-wide Real GDP Y.

options_template.text: The AD curve relates the economy-wide aggregate price level (P) to total planned real spending (C + I + G + NX) across all markets simultaneously, rather than holding other prices and income constant for one good.
options_template.feedback: Correct. AD tracks total real output demanded (Y) as the overall price level changes across the entire economy, so microeconomic ceteris paribus assumptions about fixed income and other prices do not apply.

options_template.text: The AD curve slopes downward solely because consumers substitute away from domestically produced goods toward cheaper domestic alternatives when the overall price level rises.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Micro Substitution Confusion): When the aggregate price level rises across all domestic goods simultaneously, consumers cannot substitute into other domestic goods whose prices also rose.

options_template.text: The AD curve measures nominal GDP on the horizontal axis while holding real GDP constant along the curve.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Nominal vs. Real Axis Reversal): The horizontal axis of the AD-AS diagram measures Real GDP (Y), not nominal GDP.

options_template.text: The AD curve excludes government purchases and net exports, capturing only household consumption and business investment.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Incomplete Expenditure Identity): Aggregate Demand sums all four expenditure sectors: AD = C + I + G + NX.

questions.title: Mechanism of the Wealth Effect Along AD
questions.prompt_template: According to the wealth (real-balances) effect, why does a decline in the aggregate price level (P) increase the quantity of real GDP demanded?

hints.text: Focus on how a lower price level affects the purchasing power of assets denominated in fixed dollar terms.
Consider cash, checking deposits, and nominal bonds: when P falls, what happens to their real value and to household consumption C?

options_template.text: It raises the nominal face value of cash and checking accounts held by households.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Nominal Illusion): A lower price level does not change the dollar amount printed on cash or recorded in checking accounts; it changes what those dollars can buy.

options_template.text: It increases the real purchasing power of households' fixed nominal financial assets (such as cash, checking deposits, and nominal bonds), prompting higher real consumption spending (C).
options_template.feedback: Correct. When P falls, each dollar of fixed nominal financial wealth buys more real goods and services, raising real wealth and stimulating household consumption C.

options_template.text: It automatically increases real wages across all industries, shifting the entire AD curve to the right.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Movement vs. Shift & Channel Confusion): A change in P causes a movement along AD, not a shift, and the wealth effect works through fixed nominal financial assets rather than wage mandates.

options_template.text: It lowers corporate tax rates, thereby increasing business investment spending (I).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Fiscal Policy Conflation): Tax rate changes are fiscal policy shifters of AD, not the wealth effect triggered by a lower price level.

questions.title: Transmission Channel of the Interest-Rate Effect
questions.prompt_template: Which sequence accurately traces the interest-rate effect that helps explain the downward slope of the Aggregate Demand (AD) curve?

hints.text: Start with a fall in the aggregate price level P and ask how much cash households and firms need to carry out transactions.
Less transactions demand for money puts downward pressure on interest rates r, which directly affects borrowing-sensitive spending.

options_template.text: Lower P -> higher money demand -> higher interest rates (r) -> lower investment (I).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inverted Money Demand Direction): When the price level falls, households and firms need less money—not more—for everyday transactions.

options_template.text: Higher P -> lower money demand -> lower interest rates (r) -> higher consumption (C).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inverted Price-Money Relationship): A higher price level requires more dollars for the same real transactions, increasing money demand and pushing interest rates up.

options_template.text: Lower P -> lower transactions money demand -> lower interest rates (r) -> higher business investment (I) and durable consumption (C).
options_template.feedback: Correct. A lower price level reduces the nominal money balances needed for transactions, easing credit markets, lowering interest rates r, and stimulating borrowing for investment and durable goods.

options_template.text: Lower P -> Federal Reserve automatically raises policy interest rates -> lower investment (I).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Policy Rule Confusion): The interest-rate effect along AD is a market money-demand channel, and lower prices lower—not raise—interest rates.

questions.title: Open-Economy Link in the Downward-Sloping AD Curve
questions.prompt_template: How does the exchange-rate (net export) effect reinforce the downward slope of the Aggregate Demand (AD) curve when the domestic price level falls?

hints.text: Connect the interest-rate drop from a lower P to international capital flows and the value of the domestic currency.
When the domestic currency depreciates, ask whether domestic exports become cheaper or more expensive for foreign buyers.

options_template.text: Lower domestic interest rates trigger capital inflows, appreciating the domestic currency and increasing imports.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inverted Capital Flow Direction): Lower domestic returns relative to foreign assets encourage investors to seek higher yields abroad, causing capital outflows and currency depreciation.

options_template.text: Foreign central banks immediately impose tariffs on domestic goods, reducing net exports.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Trade Policy Conflation): The exchange-rate effect operates through market interest rates and currency exchange rates, not foreign tariff retaliation.

options_template.text: Lower domestic interest rates reduce the return on domestic financial assets relative to foreign assets, causing capital outflows, domestic currency depreciation, and higher net exports (NX = X - M).
options_template.feedback: Correct. A weaker domestic currency makes domestic exports cheaper for foreign buyers and foreign imports more expensive for domestic residents, raising NX.

options_template.text: A lower domestic price level forces fixed exchange rates to appreciate, boosting exports and reducing imports.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Appreciation-Export Contradiction): Currency appreciation makes domestic exports more expensive for foreign buyers, which reduces rather than boosts net exports.

questions.topic: Why Micro Substitution Does Not Explain AD Slope
questions.title: Invalid Explanation for the Slope of AD
questions.prompt_template: Why is the microeconomic substitution effect NOT a valid explanation for the downward slope of the macroeconomic Aggregate Demand (AD) curve?

hints.text: Recall what the microeconomic substitution effect holds constant when the price of a single product rises.
If the overall price level P rises across the entire domestic economy, are other domestic goods staying cheap?

options_template.text: Because when the overall aggregate price level rises across all domestic markets at once, consumers cannot simply switch to other domestic goods whose prices have also risen.
options_template.feedback: Correct. The microeconomic substitution effect relies on one good's price rising while all other prices remain fixed, whereas AD varies the overall economy-wide price level P.

options_template.text: Because households never change their spending habits when prices change.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Overgeneralization): Households do respond to price-level changes—through the wealth, interest-rate, and exchange-rate channels—just not via domestic relative-price substitution.

options_template.text: Because the AD curve actually slopes upward in the short run.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (AD-SRAS Reversal): The AD curve slopes downward; it is the SRAS curve that slopes upward in the short run.

options_template.text: Because aggregate demand only includes capital goods purchased by firms, not consumer goods.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Expenditure Scope Error): Household consumption (C) is the largest component of AD = C + I + G + NX.

questions.title: Sticky Nominal Wages and the Upward-Sloping SRAS
questions.prompt_template: Why does the Short-Run Aggregate Supply (SRAS) curve slope upward from left to right?

hints.text: Think about what happens to a firm's profit per unit when output prices rise while nominal wages are locked into contracts.
Compare revenue per unit (P) against sticky nominal unit production costs in the short run.

options_template.text: Because higher aggregate prices immediately double the economy's physical capital stock and labor force.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Short-Run Capacity Illusion): Capital stock and labor force grow slowly over the long run (shifting LRAS), not instantaneously with short-run price changes.

options_template.text: Because nominal wages and many input prices are sticky in the short run, so a higher output price level (P) widens profit margins per unit and induces firms to expand production.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Multi-year contracts, annual salary cycles, and menu costs keep nominal unit costs temporarily fixed; when P rises, revenue per unit outpaces cost per unit, raising profitable output.

options_template.text: Because households always buy more goods when the overall price level is higher.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Demand-Supply Confusion): Household spending behavior determines the downward-sloping AD curve, not the upward-sloping SRAS curve.

options_template.text: Because nominal wages automatically adjust faster than output prices in the short run.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Reversed Stickiness): If nominal wages rose faster than output prices, profit margins would shrink and firms would cut output rather than expand it.

questions.title: Why LRAS Is Vertical at Potential Output
questions.prompt_template: Why is the Long-Run Aggregate Supply (LRAS) curve vertical at potential output (Y*)?

hints.text: Ask what happens to real profit margins if both output prices and all nominal wages double in the long run.
Long-run flexibility of nominal wages and prices means real output depends on real resources, not on P.

options_template.text: Because firms ignore changes in technology and capital accumulation in the long run.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Static LRAS Myth): LRAS does shift rightward over decades as technology and capital grow; verticality only means long-run output is independent of the price level P.

options_template.text: Because the central bank fixes real GDP directly through open-market operations.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Monetary Omnipotence): Monetary policy affects aggregate demand in the short run, whereas long-run real output is governed by real productive resources.

options_template.text: Because in the long run, nominal wages and input prices adjust proportionally with the aggregate price level, leaving real wages, relative prices, and profit margins unchanged.
options_template.feedback: Correct. When all output prices and input costs scale together in the long run, firms have no incentive to produce above or below sustainable potential output Y*.

options_template.text: Because the aggregate price level cannot change in the long run.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Fixed-Price Long Run): In the long run, the price level is fully flexible and adjusts freely to shifts in AD; it is real output that returns to Y*.

questions.topic: Potential Output & Natural Rate of Unemployment
questions.title: Determinants of Potential Output (Y*)
questions.prompt_template: Which set of factors determines the position of the vertical Long-Run Aggregate Supply (LRAS) curve at potential output (Y*)?

hints.text: Think about what determines an economy's sustainable long-run productive capacity (similar to the Macroeconomic PPF).
Distinguish real supply-side productive fundamentals from nominal prices and short-run demand shifters.

options_template.text: The aggregate price level, expected inflation, and consumer confidence.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Nominal/Demand Shifters): Expected inflation shifts SRAS, consumer confidence shifts AD, and P is on the vertical axis—none determine long-run productive capacity Y*.

options_template.text: Government deficit spending and the Federal Reserve's administered interest-rate corridor.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Short-Run Demand Policy): Fiscal and monetary policies shift AD in the short run rather than directly defining potential output Y*.

options_template.text: Short-run sticky union wage contracts and menu costs.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Short-Run Rigidity Confusion): Wage stickiness and menu costs explain the upward slope of SRAS, not the long-run productive capacity Y*.

options_template.text: The economy's labor force, physical and human capital stock, natural resources, technology, and institutions (corresponding to the natural rate of unemployment u*).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Potential output Y* reflects sustainable real productive capacity—mirroring the economy's Production Possibilities Frontier—when unemployment equals the natural rate u*.

questions.title: Recessionary Gap vs. Inflationary Gap
questions.prompt_template: How are a recessionary output gap and an inflationary output gap defined relative to potential output (Y*) and the natural rate of unemployment (u*)?

hints.text: Compare actual short-run real GDP (Y) with potential GDP (Y*) on the horizontal axis.
Remember that when real output falls below Y*, firms hire fewer workers, pushing actual unemployment u above u*.

options_template.text: A recessionary gap occurs when Y < Y* and u > u*; an inflationary gap occurs when Y > Y* and u < u*.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Producing below potential output leaves idle labor (u > u*), whereas producing above potential output overheats labor markets and pushes unemployment below the natural rate (u < u*).

options_template.text: A recessionary gap occurs when Y < Y* and u < u*; an inflationary gap occurs when Y > Y* and u > u*.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inverted Output-Unemployment Link): Output and unemployment move inversely; lower real GDP means higher—not lower—unemployment.

options_template.text: A recessionary gap occurs whenever the aggregate price level is rising; an inflationary gap occurs whenever the price level is falling.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Price-Level Gap Confusion): Output gaps are defined by comparing actual Real GDP Y to potential output Y*, not by the direction of P alone (stagflation has Y < Y* with rising P).

options_template.text: Both recessionary and inflationary gaps occur only when Y = Y*.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Equilibrium Misdefinition): When Y = Y*, the output gap is zero and the economy is in long-run macroeconomic equilibrium.

questions.title: Role of Expected Price Level (P^e) in SRAS
questions.prompt_template: In the short-run aggregate supply equation Y = Y* + gamma(P - P^e), what happens when actual prices equal expected prices (P = P^e)?

hints.text: Substitute P = P^e directly into the linear SRAS equation Y = Y* + gamma(P - P^e).
When expectations are fulfilled, there is no price surprise to distort real wages away from their long-run level.

options_template.text: Short-run real output falls to zero because firms earn zero economic profit.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Output Misconception): When P = P^e, the term gamma(P - P^e) equals zero, leaving Y = Y*, not Y = 0.

options_template.text: Short-run real output equals potential output (Y = Y*), placing the economy on the vertical LRAS curve.
options_template.feedback: Correct. When actual P matches the expected price level P^e built into nominal wage contracts, real wages equal their equilibrium level and firms produce potential output Y*.

options_template.text: Real wages fall below equilibrium, creating a permanent inflationary gap.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Surprise-Inflation Condition): Real wages W0/P fall temporarily only when actual prices exceed expected prices (P > P^e).

options_template.text: The AD curve becomes completely vertical.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Curve-Identity Confusion): P = P^e is a supply-side equilibrium condition defining where SRAS crosses vertical LRAS; it does not alter the slope of AD.

questions.title: How the Economy Self-Corrects in the Long Run
questions.prompt_template: What drives the economy's long-run self-correcting mechanism when short-run real GDP deviates from potential output (Y*)?

hints.text: Ask which curve shifts during long-run adjustment when nominal wage contracts are renegotiated.
In an inflationary gap, labor is scarce and wages rise; in a recessionary gap, high unemployment slows wage growth.

options_template.text: Automatic shifts of the vertical LRAS curve until it meets the current short-run equilibrium output.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Endogenous LRAS Myth): Long-run self-correction operates through nominal wage and price adjustment shifting SRAS, not by LRAS moving to chase short-run demand.

options_template.text: Permanent changes in the slope of the AD curve.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Slope-Adjustment Confusion): Self-correction moves the economy along a stationary AD curve as SRAS shifts.

options_template.text: Gradual adjustment of nominal wages and price expectations in response to labor-market tightness or slack, which shifts SRAS until output returns to Y*.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Tight labor markets in an inflationary gap bid up nominal wages (shifting SRAS left), while persistent slack in a recessionary gap puts downward pressure on wage growth (shifting SRAS right).

options_template.text: Mandatory legislative fiscal packages passed every quarter.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Discretionary Policy vs. Self-Correction): Self-correction refers to endogenous market adjustment of wages and prices without discretionary fiscal or monetary intervention.

questions.title: Defining Stagflation in the AD-AS Framework
questions.prompt_template: Which macroeconomic combination defines stagflation, and which type of shock generates it?

hints.text: Break down the portmanteau 'stagflation' into its two macroeconomic symptoms: stagnation + inflation.
Check which curve shift moves real output Y and the price level P in opposite directions.

options_template.text: Rising real GDP alongside falling inflation, generated by a positive supply shock.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Favorable Supply Shock Confusion): Rising output with falling prices is a favorable productivity/supply boom, the exact opposite of stagflation.

options_template.text: Falling real GDP alongside falling inflation, generated by a negative demand shock.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Demand-Driven Recession Confusion): A negative demand shock lowers both output and the price level (recession with disinflation/deflation), not stagflation.

options_template.text: Rising real GDP alongside rising inflation, generated by a positive demand shock.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Overheating Expansion Confusion): Simultaneous increases in Y and P represent an expansionary inflationary gap, not stagnation.

options_template.text: Falling real GDP (rising unemployment) alongside a rising aggregate price level, generated by an adverse supply shock shifting SRAS leftward.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Stagflation combines economic stagnation (Y < Y*, u > u*) with higher inflation (P > P*), caused by cost spikes that shift SRAS leftward.

questions.title: Canonical FRED Indicators for AD-AS Diagnostics
questions.prompt_template: Which pairing accurately matches the three canonical St. Louis Fed FRED series used to diagnose AD-AS business cycle shocks?

hints.text: Recall the three FRED series highlighted in the Chapter 9 FRED Data Diagnostics box.
Remember that Real GDP is measured quarterly, whereas CPI and the unemployment rate are measured monthly.

options_template.text: GDPC1 = Real GDP (quarterly); CPIAUCSL = Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (monthly); UNRATE = Civilian Unemployment Rate (monthly).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Macroeconomists pair quarterly real output (GDPC1) with monthly consumer prices (CPIAUCSL) and monthly unemployment (UNRATE) to distinguish demand shocks from supply shocks.

options_template.text: GDPC1 = Nominal GDP (monthly); CPIAUCSL = Core Producer Price Index (quarterly); UNRATE = Labor Force Participation Rate (annual).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Series Definition & Frequency Error): GDPC1 is real (chained 2017 dollars) and quarterly; CPIAUCSL is headline all-items CPI and monthly; UNRATE is the monthly unemployment rate.

options_template.text: GDPC1 = Government Debt (quarterly); CPIAUCSL = Corporate Profit Index (monthly); UNRATE = Unit Labor Cost (quarterly).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Acronym Misinterpretation): GDPC1 measures Real Gross Domestic Product, CPIAUCSL measures the Consumer Price Index, and UNRATE measures the Civilian Unemployment Rate.

options_template.text: GDPC1 = Real GDP (monthly); CPIAUCSL = GDP Deflator (quarterly); UNRATE = Natural Rate of Unemployment (monthly).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Frequency & Index Swap): Real GDP (GDPC1) is reported quarterly, CPIAUCSL is the monthly CPI (not GDP deflator), and UNRATE is actual—not natural—unemployment.

questions.topic: Movement Along AD vs. Shift of AD
questions.title: Graphical Effect of a Lower Aggregate Price Level
questions.prompt_template: In the Aggregate Demand diagram, if the domestic aggregate price level falls from P_A to P_B while all non-price spending determinants remain unchanged, how is this represented?

hints.text: Check whether the changing variable (the aggregate price level P) is already on one of the axes of the AD graph.
Changes in an axis variable produce a movement along the curve; changes in an outside determinant shift the curve.

options_template.text: As a rightward shift of the entire AD curve from AD_1 to AD_2.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Endogenous Price Shift Error): Never treat a change in the vertical-axis variable P as a shifter of the AD curve.

options_template.text: As a downward movement along the stationary AD_1 curve to a higher level of real GDP demanded.
options_template.feedback: Correct. A lower price level P induces higher planned real spending via the wealth, interest-rate, and exchange-rate effects, tracing a movement down along the existing AD curve.

options_template.text: As a leftward shift of the entire AD curve because lower prices reduce firm revenues.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Revenue-Spending Confusion): Lower P raises real balances and lowers interest rates, increasing—not decreasing—real output demanded along AD.

options_template.text: As a vertical shift of the LRAS curve to the right.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Nominal-Capacity Confusion): Changes in the price level P do not alter the economy's long-run potential output Y*.

questions.title: Fiscal Expansion at a Constant Price Level
questions.prompt_template: Suppose Congress increases government purchases (G) while the aggregate price level is held constant at P_B. How does this appear on the AD diagram, and what is its short-run effect in the full AD-SRAS model?

hints.text: Ask whether higher G changes planned spending at every price level P.
Once AD shifts right, trace the new intersection with the upward-sloping SRAS curve.

options_template.text: AD shifts horizontally rightward from AD_1 to AD_2; in the short-run AD-SRAS equilibrium, both real output (Y) and the price level (P) rise.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Higher autonomous spending G raises planned expenditure at every price level (shifting AD right), moving the economy up along SRAS so both Y and P increase.

options_template.text: The economy moves down along AD_1; in the short run, real output rises while the price level falls.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Movement vs. Shift Error): Higher government purchases is a non-price determinant that shifts AD rightward rather than moving along AD_1.

options_template.text: SRAS shifts rightward while AD remains unchanged; real output rises and the price level falls.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Demand-Supply Shifter Swap): Government purchases of goods and services directly shift Aggregate Demand, not Short-Run Aggregate Supply.

options_template.text: AD shifts leftward from AD_1 to AD_2; both real output and the price level fall.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Reversed Shift Direction): An increase in G adds to total planned spending (C + I + G + NX), shifting AD rightward, not leftward.

questions.title: Higher Policy Interest Rates and Planned Investment
questions.prompt_template: When the Federal Reserve raises its administered interest-rate corridor—pushing 30-year mortgage rates sharply higher—which curve shifts in the AD-AS diagram, and what happens to short-run equilibrium?

hints.text: Identify which components of AD = C + I + G + NX are most sensitive to mortgage and borrowing rates.
Because the central bank raises rates independently of a change in P, the entire AD curve shifts.

options_template.text: SRAS shifts leftward, raising the price level and reducing real GDP.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Policy-Channel Mismatch): Higher mortgage and borrowing rates reduce planned investment (I) and durable consumption (C), which shifts AD rather than SRAS.

options_template.text: The economy moves upward along a stationary AD curve, leaving planned spending unchanged at each price level.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Endogenous vs. Policy Rate Confusion): A discretionary Federal Reserve rate hike changes interest rates at every given price level P, shifting the entire AD curve.

options_template.text: AD shifts leftward, reducing both short-run real GDP (Y) and the aggregate price level (P) relative to baseline.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Higher borrowing costs reduce residential investment (I) and durable goods consumption (C) at every price level, shifting AD leftward and cooling both output and prices.

options_template.text: LRAS shifts leftward immediately, permanently lowering potential output Y*.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Short-Run vs. Long-Run Confusion): Monetary tightening is a demand-side stabilization tool and does not directly destroy the economy's physical capital or labor force.

questions.title: Foreign GDP Boom or Currency Depreciation
questions.prompt_template: Suppose major U.S. trading partners experience a rapid economic expansion (higher foreign GDP) at every U.S. price level. How does this affect the U.S. AD-SRAS equilibrium in the short run?

hints.text: Determine how higher foreign income affects U.S. exports (X) and therefore net exports (NX = X - M).
Trace a rightward shift of AD along an upward-sloping SRAS curve.

options_template.text: U.S. AD shifts leftward because foreign buyers consume more of their own goods; U.S. Y and P fall.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Reversed Trade Effect): Higher foreign income raises foreign demand for U.S. exports (X), increasing U.S. net exports (NX) and shifting AD rightward.

options_template.text: U.S. AD shifts rightward due to higher net exports (NX), moving the economy up along SRAS so U.S. real GDP (Y) and the price level (P) both rise.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Faster foreign growth boosts U.S. exports at every domestic price level, shifting AD rightward and increasing both short-run Y and P.

options_template.text: U.S. SRAS shifts rightward while AD stays fixed, raising Y and lowering P.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Demand-Supply Shifter Swap): Higher foreign demand for domestic exports alters planned spending (NX in AD), not domestic unit production costs (SRAS).

options_template.text: U.S. LRAS shifts rightward immediately because exports are part of potential GDP.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Demand vs. Capacity Error): Export demand is an expenditure component of AD, not an expansion of domestic productive capacity Y*.

questions.topic: Movement Along SRAS vs. Shift of SRAS
questions.title: Distinguishing SRAS Movements from SRAS Shifts
questions.prompt_template: Which event causes an upward movement ALONG a stationary SRAS curve rather than a shift of the SRAS curve itself?

hints.text: Remember that a movement along SRAS is triggered only by a change in the aggregate price level P (typically caused by a shift in AD).
Eliminate any option that directly changes unit production costs or expected prices.

options_template.text: A surge in household consumer confidence that shifts AD rightward, raising the aggregate price level P.
options_template.feedback: Correct. A rightward shift of AD raises the aggregate price level P; holding nominal wages and input costs fixed, firms move upward along the existing SRAS curve to expand output.

options_template.text: A sudden spike in global crude oil and electricity prices.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Input-Cost Shifter): Higher energy prices raise unit production costs at every price level, shifting the entire SRAS curve leftward (upward).

options_template.text: A newly negotiated economy-wide increase in nominal wages.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Wage-Cost Shifter): Higher nominal wages increase unit labor costs at every price level, shifting SRAS leftward.

options_template.text: An economy-wide breakthrough in total factor productivity.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Productivity Shifter): Higher productivity lowers unit costs at every price level, shifting both SRAS and LRAS rightward.

questions.title: Graphical Impact of a Commodity Price Spike
questions.prompt_template: Starting from long-run equilibrium E_1 = (Y*, P_1), a sharp spike in global energy and raw-material prices hits the economy. How does the AD-AS diagram change in the short run?

hints.text: Ask whether higher energy costs shift AD or SRAS, and in which direction.
Trace the new intersection of the shifted SRAS curve with the stationary downward-sloping AD curve.

options_template.text: AD shifts leftward, lowering both Y and P.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Demand-Shock Misclassification): Energy and commodity prices are production inputs that shift SRAS, not primarily AD.

options_template.text: SRAS shifts rightward, raising Y above Y* and lowering P below P_1.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Reversed Supply Shift): Higher input costs reduce profitability at each price level, shifting SRAS leftward (upward), not rightward.

options_template.text: SRAS shifts leftward (upward) from SRAS_1 to SRAS_2, moving equilibrium up along AD so real output falls (Y_2 < Y*) while the price level rises (P_2 > P_1).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Higher unit production costs shift SRAS leftward, creating stagflation: a recessionary gap (Y_2 < Y*, u > u*) combined with a higher price level (P_2 > P_1).

options_template.text: Both AD and SRAS shift rightward, leaving the price level unchanged.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Unrelated Dual Shift): An energy cost spike does not boost autonomous spending or lower production costs.

questions.title: Long-Run and Short-Run Effects of Productivity Growth
questions.prompt_template: Suppose a major wave of technological innovation permanently raises total factor productivity across manufacturing, logistics, and software. Which curves shift in the AD-AS diagram?

hints.text: Consider how higher output per worker affects both short-run unit labor costs and long-run potential output Y*.
Match this to an outward shift of the Macroeconomic Production Possibilities Frontier.

options_template.text: Only AD shifts rightward, leaving LRAS unchanged.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Demand-Only View): Higher productivity directly lowers unit labor costs and expands the economy's sustainable productive capacity.

options_template.text: Both SRAS and vertical LRAS shift rightward, allowing higher potential output (Y*) with downward pressure on unit costs and prices.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Total factor productivity gains reduce unit production costs in the short run (shifting SRAS right) and expand sustainable real capacity in the long run (shifting LRAS right).

options_template.text: SRAS shifts leftward while LRAS shifts rightward.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Conflicting Supply Directions): Higher productivity lowers unit costs, which shifts SRAS rightward—not leftward.

options_template.text: Only SRAS shifts rightward; LRAS can never shift.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Immovable LRAS Fallacy): LRAS is vertical with respect to P, but it shifts rightward over time with capital deepening, labor growth, and technological progress.

questions.topic: Expected Price Level Shift of SRAS
questions.title: Higher Inflation Expectations and Wage Bargaining
questions.prompt_template: If workers and firms suddenly expect a higher aggregate price level (P^e increases) and negotiate higher nominal wages today, what happens in the AD-AS diagram in the short run?

hints.text: Look at the equation SRAS: P = P^e + (1/gamma)(Y - Y*). What happens to the vertical intercept when P^e rises?
Higher nominal wage settlements raise unit labor costs today, shifting SRAS leftward.

options_template.text: SRAS shifts leftward (upward), raising the actual price level P and lowering short-run real output Y.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Higher expected prices lead to higher nominal wage settlements today, raising unit labor costs at every P and shifting SRAS leftward—creating higher actual prices and lower output.

options_template.text: SRAS shifts rightward (downward), lowering P and raising Y.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inverted Wage-Cost Direction): Higher nominal wages raise production costs and reduce profitable output at each P, shifting SRAS leftward.

options_template.text: LRAS shifts leftward because workers expect higher prices.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Nominal Expectations vs. Real Capacity): Price expectations are nominal and shift SRAS, not the economy's real productive capacity LRAS.

options_template.text: Neither AD nor SRAS shifts until actual inflation occurs.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ignoring Forward-Looking Contracts): Because nominal wages are set in advance based on P^e, higher inflation expectations shift SRAS immediately.

questions.title: Three-Point Trajectory E_1 -> E_2 -> E_3
questions.prompt_template: Starting at long-run equilibrium E_1 = (Y*, P_1), an investment boom shifts AD rightward to AD_2. In the absence of policy intervention, how does the economy travel from E_1 to short-run equilibrium E_2 and then to long-run equilibrium E_3?

hints.text: Trace Figure 3 Panel A: first find the intersection of AD_2 and SRAS_1 (E_2), then determine which way SRAS shifts when u < u*.
Long-run equilibrium E_3 must lie on both AD_2 and vertical LRAS (Y*).

options_template.text: E_1 -> E_2: Y rises above Y* and P rises to P_2; E_2 -> E_3: rising nominal wages shift SRAS leftward until Y returns to Y* at a permanently higher price level P_3 > P_2.
options_template.feedback: Correct. The inflationary gap at E_2 creates tight labor markets and erodes real wages (P_2 > P^e), driving nominal wages up and shifting SRAS leftward to E_3 = (Y*, P_3).

options_template.text: E_1 -> E_2: Y rises above Y* and P falls; E_2 -> E_3: AD shifts back leftward to E_1.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (AD-Reversal Myth): A positive demand shock raises P at E_2, and long-run self-correction operates through SRAS shifting leftward—not AD returning to AD_1.

options_template.text: E_1 -> E_2: Y rises above Y* and P rises; E_2 -> E_3: falling nominal wages shift SRAS rightward so Y expands further.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inverted Wage Adjustment): Tight labor markets (u < u*) push nominal wages up, not down, shifting SRAS leftward.

options_template.text: E_1 -> E_2: Y stays fixed at Y* while P rises immediately to P_3.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Instantaneous Long-Run Adjustment): Because nominal wages are sticky in the short run, the economy first moves along SRAS_1 to E_2 (Y_2 > Y*) before self-correcting to E_3.

questions.title: Recessionary Gap Adjustment Path
questions.prompt_template: Starting from long-run equilibrium E_1 = (Y*, P_1), a collapse in consumer confidence shifts AD leftward to AD_2. Assuming no policy intervention, what is the long-run self-correcting path?

hints.text: First locate the short-run intersection of AD_2 (shifted left) and SRAS_1, then ask how high unemployment affects nominal wage growth.
As unit labor costs fall, SRAS shifts rightward along AD_2 until Y = Y*.

options_template.text: Short-run output falls below Y* and P falls; over time, high unemployment slows nominal wage growth, shifting SRAS rightward until output returns to Y* at an even lower price level P_3 < P_2.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Persistent labor-market slack (u > u*) eventually reduces nominal wage growth and unit production costs, shifting SRAS rightward along AD_2 back to potential output Y* at a lower P_3.

options_template.text: Short-run output falls below Y* and P rises; over time, SRAS shifts leftward back to Y*.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Supply-Shock Confusion): A negative demand shock lowers—not raises—the price level P, and returning to Y* requires SRAS to shift rightward.

options_template.text: Short-run output falls below Y* and P falls; over time, LRAS shifts leftward to match the lower output.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (LRAS Chasing AD): Self-correction closes a recessionary gap via falling nominal wage growth shifting SRAS rightward, not by LRAS collapsing to Y_2.

options_template.text: Short-run output rises above Y* and P falls; over time, nominal wages rise to restore Y*.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Reversed Output Direction): A leftward AD shift reduces planned spending and output below Y*, creating a recessionary gap.

questions.title: Comparing Output-Price Co-Movement Across Shocks
questions.prompt_template: In the short-run AD-SRAS model, how does the directional co-movement of real GDP (Y) and the aggregate price level (P) distinguish a pure demand shock from a pure supply shock?

hints.text: Think about which stationary curve the economy slides along during each type of shock.
Sliding along upward-sloping SRAS means ΔY and ΔP share the same sign; sliding along downward-sloping AD means they have opposite signs.

options_template.text: Both demand shocks and supply shocks always move Y and P in the same direction.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Uniform Co-Movement Myth): Only demand shocks move Y and P in the same direction along upward-sloping SRAS.

options_template.text: A pure demand shock moves Y and P in the same direction, whereas a pure supply shock moves Y and P in opposite directions.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Shifting AD moves equilibrium along upward-sloping SRAS (so Y and P move together), whereas shifting SRAS moves equilibrium along downward-sloping AD (so Y and P move oppositely).

options_template.text: A pure demand shock moves Y and P in opposite directions, whereas a pure supply shock moves Y and P in the same direction.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Reversed Co-Movement Rule): Check the slopes: moving along upward-sloping SRAS (AD shock) gives positive co-movement; moving along downward-sloping AD (SRAS shock) gives negative co-movement.

options_template.text: A pure demand shock changes only P while leaving Y unchanged in the short run.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Long-Run Neutrality Applied to Short Run): In the short run, SRAS is upward-sloping, so an AD shift changes both Y and P.

questions.title: Combined Rightward AD Shift and Leftward SRAS Shift
questions.prompt_template: Suppose an economy simultaneously experiences a rightward shift of AD (e.g., fiscal stimulus) and a leftward shift of SRAS (e.g., global energy and supply-chain bottlenecks). What can be predicted with certainty about the new short-run equilibrium?

hints.text: List the directional effect of each shock separately on Y and on P, then combine them.
AD right: Y↑, P↑. SRAS left: Y↓, P↑. Which variable moves in the same direction under both shocks?

options_template.text: Real GDP (Y) unambiguously rises, while the change in the price level (P) is ambiguous.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Swapped Ambiguity): Rightward AD pushes Y up while leftward SRAS pushes Y down, making Y—not P—ambiguous.

options_template.text: Both real GDP (Y) and the price level (P) unambiguously fall.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ignoring AD Expansion): Both shifts push the price level upward, so P cannot fall.

options_template.text: The aggregate price level (P) unambiguously rises, while the net change in real GDP (Y) is ambiguous without knowing the relative sizes of the two shifts.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Both a rightward AD shift and a leftward SRAS shift exert upward pressure on P, whereas they pull Y in opposite directions.

options_template.text: Both real GDP (Y) and the price level (P) remain completely unchanged.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Exact Cancellation Assumption): Even if output effects happened to offset, both shifts reinforce each other to push P higher.

questions.title: Diagnosing Output Gaps on the AD-SRAS-LRAS Graph
questions.prompt_template: On an AD-SRAS-LRAS diagram, the short-run intersection of AD and SRAS lies strictly to the left of the vertical LRAS curve. Which statement accurately describes this economy?

hints.text: Real GDP (Y) increases from left to right along the horizontal axis.
If actual Y is to the left of Y*, compare Y to Y* and then infer whether unemployment u is above or below u*.

options_template.text: The economy has an inflationary gap (Y > Y*) and actual unemployment is below the natural rate (u < u*).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Left-Right Axis Reversal): Points to the left of Y* have lower real GDP (Y < Y*), not higher real GDP.

options_template.text: The economy is in long-run equilibrium with zero cyclical unemployment.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Equilibrium Misreading): Long-run equilibrium requires AD, SRAS, and LRAS to intersect at the same point on Y*.

options_template.text: The economy has a recessionary gap (Y < Y*) and actual unemployment exceeds the natural rate (u > u*).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Any short-run equilibrium to the left of vertical LRAS represents real output below potential (Y < Y*), implying idle capacity and cyclical unemployment (u > u*).

options_template.text: The economy is producing beyond its sustainable capacity, putting immediate upward pressure on nominal wages.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Overheating Confusion): Producing to the left of LRAS means slack capacity and downward—not upward—pressure on nominal wage growth.

questions.title: Quantifying a Movement Along Linear AD
questions.prompt_template: Suppose an economy's Aggregate Demand curve is given by Y = 48 - 0.25P, where Y is real GDP in trillions of chained 2017 dollars and P is the price index. If the aggregate price level falls from P = 120 to P = 100, what is the resulting change in real GDP demanded along this AD curve?

hints.text: Substitute P = 120 and P = 100 separately into Y = 48 - 0.25P, then compute Y_B - Y_A.
Alternatively, use Delta Y = -0.25 * Delta P with Delta P = 100 - 120 = -20.

options_template.text: +$5.0 trillion (from $18.0 trillion to $23.0 trillion)
-$5.0 trillion (from $23.0 trillion to $18.0 trillion)
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sign Reversal): Falling prices increase—not decrease—real GDP demanded along a downward-sloping AD curve (Delta Y = -0.25 * (-20) = +5.0).

options_template.text: +$20.0 trillion (equal to the 20-point drop in the price index)
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted Slope Coefficient): You must multiply the price change (-20) by the slope coefficient (-0.25), not treat Delta P directly as Delta Y.

options_template.text: +$8.0 trillion (from $15.0 trillion to $23.0 trillion)
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Arithmetic Multiplication Error): 0.25 * 120 = 30 (giving Y_A = 48 - 30 = 18), not 33.

questions.title: Calculating Output After an Autonomous Spending Shift
questions.prompt_template: Baseline Aggregate Demand is Y = 40 - 0.2P (with Y in trillions of dollars). Suppose an autonomous surge in business investment raises A_0 by $6.0 trillion at every price level. What is the new quantity of real GDP demanded at an unchanged price level of P = 100?

hints.text: Write the new AD equation by adding +6 to the autonomous intercept A_0 = 40.
Evaluate Y = 46 - 0.2P at P = 100.

options_template.text: $20.0 trillion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Unshifted Baseline): $20.0 trillion is the original output at P = 100 (40 - 0.2(100) = 20) before adding the $6.0 trillion autonomous shift.

options_template.text: $26.0 trillion
options_template.feedback: Correct. The shifted AD curve is Y = (40 + 6) - 0.2P = 46 - 0.2P. At P = 100, Y = 46 - 0.2(100) = 46 - 20 = $26.0 trillion.

options_template.text: $14.0 trillion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Reversed Shift Sign): An increase in autonomous investment adds +6.0 to A_0 rather than subtracting 6.0.

options_template.text: $21.2 trillion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Multiplying Shift by Slope): In Y = A_0 - beta*P, an autonomous spending change Delta A_0 shifts Y horizontally by the full +$6.0 trillion, not by 0.2 * 6.0 = $1.2 trillion.

questions.title: Calculating Short-Run Output from a Price Surprise
questions.prompt_template: Suppose Short-Run Aggregate Supply is given by Y = Y* + gamma(P - P^e), where potential output is Y* = $20.0 trillion, gamma = 0.25, and the expected price level is P^e = 100. If the actual price level turns out to be P = 112, what is short-run real output (Y)?

hints.text: First compute the price surprise (P - P^e) = 112 - 100.
Multiply the price surprise by gamma = 0.25 and add the result to Y* = 20.

options_template.text: $17.0 trillion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Reversed Price Surprise Sign): Because P > P^e (112 > 100), real wages fall temporarily and firms expand output above Y* (20 + 3 = 23), rather than cutting output to 17.

options_template.text: $32.0 trillion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted Slope Parameter gamma): Adding (P - P^e) = 12 directly to Y* = 20 ignores the slope parameter gamma = 0.25.

options_template.text: $23.0 trillion
options_template.feedback: Correct. Substituting into Y = 20 + 0.25(112 - 100) gives Y = 20 + 0.25(12) = 20 + 3 = $23.0 trillion.

options_template.text: $20.0 trillion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Long-Run Assumption in Short Run): Output equals Y* = 20 only when P = P^e or in the long run after nominal wages fully adjust.

questions.title: Algebraic Equilibrium Output and Price Level
questions.prompt_template: Consider a macroeconomy described by AD: P = 160 - 4Y and SRAS: P = 40 + 2Y (with Y in trillions of dollars and P as a price index). What is the short-run macroeconomic equilibrium (Y_1, P_1)?

hints.text: Set the AD price equation equal to the SRAS price equation: 160 - 4Y = 40 + 2Y.
Solve for Y first, then plug Y back into both equations to verify you obtain the same P.

options_template.text: Y_1 = $20.0 trillion, P_1 = 80
options_template.feedback: Correct. Setting 160 - 4Y = 40 + 2Y gives 120 = 6Y, so Y_1 = 20. Substituting into either curve yields P_1 = 160 - 4(20) = 80 (and 40 + 2(20) = 80).

options_template.text: Y_1 = $20.0 trillion, P_1 = 100
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Back-Substitution Arithmetic Error): With Y_1 = 20, P_1 = 40 + 2(20) = 80, not 100.

options_template.text: Y_1 = $60.0 trillion, P_1 = 80
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Slope Subtraction Error): Combining -4Y and +2Y gives 6Y = 120 (Y = 20), not 2Y = 120 (Y = 60).

options_template.text: Y_1 = $15.0 trillion, P_1 = 100
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Intercept Addition Error): Subtracting 40 from 160 gives 120, not 90.

questions.title: Equilibrium and Output Gap After an AD Surge
questions.prompt_template: An economy begins in long-run equilibrium with AD_1: P = 180 - 4Y, SRAS_1: P = 20 + 4Y, and LRAS: Y* = $20.0 trillion (so E_1 = (20, 100)). A business investment boom shifts Aggregate Demand to AD_2: P = 204 - 4Y. What are the new short-run equilibrium (Y_2, P_2) and the resulting output gap?

hints.text: Equate the new AD_2 (P = 204 - 4Y) with the unchanged SRAS_1 (P = 20 + 4Y).
After solving for Y_2, compute P_2 and subtract Y* = 20 to find the output gap.

options_template.text: Y_2 = $26.0 trillion, P_2 = 100; inflationary gap = +$6.0 trillion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Fixed-Price Keynesian Assumption): Holding P fixed at 100 ignores the upward-sloping SRAS curve, which causes P to rise and dampens the short-run output expansion.

options_template.text: Y_2 = $23.0 trillion, P_2 = 124; inflationary gap = +$3.0 trillion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Mixing Short-Run Y with Long-Run P): At Y_2 = 23, P_2 = 204 - 4(23) = 112; P = 124 is the long-run price level at Y* = 20.

options_template.text: Y_2 = $22.0 trillion, P_2 = 116; inflationary gap = +$2.0 trillion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Arithmetic Division Error): 204 - 20 = 184, and 184 / 8 = 23, not 22.

options_template.text: Y_2 = $23.0 trillion, P_2 = 112; inflationary gap = +$3.0 trillion
options_template.feedback: Correct. Setting AD_2 = SRAS_1 gives 204 - 4Y = 20 + 4Y -> 184 = 8Y -> Y_2 = 23. Then P_2 = 204 - 4(23) = 112, and the inflationary gap is Y_2 - Y* = 23 - 20 = +$3.0 trillion.

questions.title: Long-Run Price Level After a Positive Demand Shock
questions.prompt_template: Continuing from an economy with AD_2: P = 204 - 4Y, SRAS_1: P = 20 + 4Y, and potential output Y* = $20.0 trillion, suppose the economy self-corrects in the long run with no policy intervention. What is the new long-run equilibrium (Y_3, P_3)?

hints.text: In long-run equilibrium, real output must return to potential output Y* = 20 while remaining on AD_2.
Plug Y = 20 directly into AD_2: P = 204 - 4Y.

options_template.text: Y_3 = $23.0 trillion, P_3 = 112
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Stopping at Short-Run Equilibrium): (23, 112) is the short-run inflationary-gap equilibrium E_2 before nominal wages adjust.

options_template.text: Y_3 = $20.0 trillion, P_3 = 124
options_template.feedback: Correct. In the long run, rising nominal wages shift SRAS leftward until output returns to Y_3 = Y* = 20 along AD_2. Substituting Y = 20 into AD_2 gives P_3 = 204 - 4(20) = 124 (with SRAS_2: P = 44 + 4Y).

options_template.text: Y_3 = $20.0 trillion, P_3 = 112
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Frozen Price Level): As SRAS shifts leftward to close the inflationary gap, the economy moves up along AD_2, pushing P higher from 112 to 124.

options_template.text: Y_3 = $20.0 trillion, P_3 = 100
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Reverting to Original Equilibrium): Because AD remains at AD_2, self-correction restores potential output Y* = 20 at a permanently higher price level, not at P_1 = 100.

questions.title: Calculating Stagflation Equilibrium and Recessionary Gap
questions.prompt_template: An economy starts in long-run equilibrium with AD_1: P = 170 - 3Y, SRAS_1: P = 20 + 2Y, and Y* = $30.0 trillion (P_1 = 80). An energy price spike shifts SRAS upward by 15 index points to SRAS_2: P = 35 + 2Y. What are the new short-run equilibrium (Y_2, P_2) and output gap?

hints.text: Equate AD_1 (P = 170 - 3Y) with the shifted supply curve SRAS_2 (P = 35 + 2Y).
Solve 135 = 5Y for Y_2, compute P_2, and then evaluate Y_2 - Y*.

options_template.text: Y_2 = $27.0 trillion, P_2 = 95; recessionary gap = -$3.0 trillion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Adding Full Cost Shift to Initial Price): Adding the full 15-point SRAS shift to P_1 = 80 ignores the downward-sloping AD curve; actual P_2 rises by only 9 points to 89.

options_template.text: Y_2 = $33.0 trillion, P_2 = 89; inflationary gap = +$3.0 trillion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Reversed Output Direction): An adverse supply shock reduces output below Y* = 30; it cannot expand output to 33.

options_template.text: Y_2 = $27.0 trillion, P_2 = 89; recessionary gap = -$3.0 trillion
options_template.feedback: Correct. Setting 170 - 3Y = 35 + 2Y gives 135 = 5Y -> Y_2 = 27. Substituting into AD_1 gives P_2 = 170 - 3(27) = 89, and the recessionary gap is 27 - 30 = -$3.0 trillion.

options_template.text: Y_2 = $25.0 trillion, P_2 = 95; recessionary gap = -$5.0 trillion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Slope Addition Error): Combining -3Y and +2Y yields 5Y = 135 (Y = 27), not 5Y = 125.

questions.title: Computing Percentage Output Gap and Price-Level Change
questions.prompt_template: An economy begins in long-run equilibrium at potential output Y* = $20.0 trillion and price index P_1 = 100. Following an adverse supply shock, short-run equilibrium moves to Y_2 = $18.0 trillion and P_2 = 106. What are the percentage output gap and the percentage change in the price level?

hints.text: Use the standard formulas: % Output Gap = [(Y_2 - Y*) / Y*] * 100% and %ΔP = [(P_2 - P_1) / P_1] * 100%.
Remember to divide the output gap by potential output Y* = 20, not by 18.

options_template.text: Output gap = -10%; price level change = +6%
options_template.feedback: Correct. The percentage output gap is [(18 - 20) / 20] * 100% = -10%, and the price level rises by [(106 - 100) / 100] * 100% = +6%.

options_template.text: Output gap = -2%; price level change = +6%
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Confusing Dollar Gap with Percentage Gap): -$2.0 trillion is the dollar output gap; dividing by Y* = $20.0 trillion yields -10%, not -2%.

options_template.text: Output gap = +10%; price level change = -6%
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inverted Signs): Actual output fell below potential (negative gap) while the price level rose (positive inflation).

options_template.text: Output gap = -11.1%; price level change = +5.7%
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ending-Value Base Error): Standard percentage output gaps divide by potential output Y* = 20 (not Y_2 = 18), and inflation divides by the initial price index P_1 = 100 (not P_2 = 106).

questions.title: Quantifying Wage Disinflation Needed to Restore Y*
questions.prompt_template: An economy starts in long-run equilibrium with AD_1: P = 150 - 3Y, SRAS_1: P = 30 + 3Y, and Y* = $20.0 trillion (P_1 = 90). A negative demand shock shifts AD to AD_2: P = 132 - 3Y (creating a short-run recessionary equilibrium at Y_2 = 17, P_2 = 81). For long-run self-correction to restore Y* = 20 along AD_2, what will the new long-run price level P_3 be, and by how much must the SRAS vertical intercept fall?

hints.text: First find P_3 by evaluating AD_2: P = 132 - 3Y at Y* = 20.
Then solve 72 = c + 3(20) to find the new SRAS vertical intercept c and compare it to 30.

options_template.text: P_3 = 81; SRAS vertical intercept falls by 9 index points (from 30 to 21)
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Stopping at Short-Run Price Level): P = 81 is the short-run equilibrium price at Y_2 = 17; moving down along AD_2 to Y* = 20 lowers P further to 72.

options_template.text: P_3 = 90; SRAS vertical intercept does not change (stays at 30)
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (No-Adjustment Error): Keeping the SRAS intercept at 30 traps the economy in the recessionary gap at Y_2 = 17.

options_template.text: P_3 = 72; SRAS vertical intercept falls by 9 index points (from 30 to 21)
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Half-Shift Error): Plugging Y = 20 into P = 21 + 3Y gives P = 81, not 72; the vertical intercept must fall by the full 18-point vertical drop of AD.

options_template.text: P_3 = 72; SRAS vertical intercept falls by 18 index points (from 30 to 12)
options_template.feedback: Correct. At Y* = 20 on AD_2, P_3 = 132 - 3(20) = 72. For SRAS_2: P = c + 3Y to pass through (20, 72), we need 72 = c + 60 -> c = 12, a drop of 18 points from 30.

questions.title: Equilibrium Under Combined Demand and Supply Shocks
questions.prompt_template: An economy begins at long-run equilibrium with AD_1: P = 160 - 2Y, SRAS_1: P = 40 + 2Y, and Y* = $30.0 trillion (P_1 = 100). Suppose fiscal expansion shifts AD upward to AD_2: P = 180 - 2Y while an energy shock simultaneously shifts SRAS upward to SRAS_2: P = 52 + 2Y. What is the new short-run equilibrium (Y_2, P_2)?

hints.text: Equate the two NEW curves directly: 180 - 2Y = 52 + 2Y.
Solve 128 = 4Y for Y_2, then substitute Y_2 into either new equation to get P_2.

options_template.text: Y_2 = $30.0 trillion, P_2 = 116
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Assumed Exact Output Cancellation): Because the AD upward shift (+20) is larger than the SRAS upward shift (+12), output expands above Y* = 30 to 32.

options_template.text: Y_2 = $32.0 trillion, P_2 = 116
options_template.feedback: Correct. Equating AD_2 = SRAS_2 gives 180 - 2Y = 52 + 2Y -> 128 = 4Y -> Y_2 = 32. Substituting into AD_2 yields P_2 = 180 - 2(32) = 116 (and 52 + 2(32) = 116).

options_template.text: Y_2 = $35.0 trillion, P_2 = 110
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ignoring the SRAS Shock): (35, 110) is the intersection of AD_2 with the original SRAS_1 (40 + 2Y), omitting the +12 supply shock.

options_template.text: Y_2 = $28.0 trillion, P_2 = 124
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Reversed Net Shift): Y = 28 would occur if the supply shock exceeded the demand shock, whereas here 180 - 52 = 128 > 120.

questions.title: Dampened Fiscal Multiplier with Upward-Sloping SRAS
questions.prompt_template: Using the short-run comparative-statics formula dY/dG = D_G / (1 - D_P * S_Y), suppose the fixed-price Keynesian multiplier is D_G = 3.0, the AD price sensitivity is D_P = -0.25, and the SRAS slope is S_Y = 2.0. What is the short-run fiscal output multiplier dY/dG?

hints.text: Pay careful attention to the negative sign on D_P = -0.25 when evaluating 1 - D_P * S_Y.
First compute D_P * S_Y = (-0.25)(2.0) = -0.5, then subtract it from 1 before dividing into D_G = 3.0.

options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ignoring Price-Level Crowding Out): 3.0 is the fixed-price Keynesian Cross multiplier (S_Y = 0), which ignores that rising P dampens output when SRAS slopes upward.
Diagnostic fallacy (Denominator Sign Error): Because D_P = -0.25 is negative, 1 - D_P*S_Y = 1 - (-0.5) = 1.5, not 1 - 0.5 = 0.5.
Correct. Compute the denominator: 1 - (-0.25)(2.0) = 1 - (-0.5) = 1.5. Thus dY/dG = 3.0 / 1.5 = 2.0, which is smaller than the fixed-price multiplier of 3.0.
Diagnostic fallacy (Omitting D_P in Denominator): Dividing D_G = 3.0 by (1 + S_Y) = 3.0 omits the AD price sensitivity D_P = -0.25.

questions.topic: Short-Run vs. Long-Run Fiscal Price Multiplier
questions.title: Comparing Short-Run and Long-Run Price Effects of ΔG
questions.prompt_template: In the differentiable AD-AS system, the short-run price multiplier is dP/dG = (S_Y * D_G) / (1 - D_P * S_Y), while the long-run price effect along vertical LRAS is lim (S_Y -> inf) dP/dG = -D_G / D_P. Given D_G = 3.0, D_P = -0.5, and S_Y = 1.0, what are the short-run and long-run price multipliers (dP/dG)?

hints.text: Evaluate both formulas separately using D_G = 3.0, D_P = -0.5, and S_Y = 1.0.
Check your intuition: should a permanent AD increase raise P by more in the long run than in the short run?

options_template.text: Short-run dP/dG = 2.0; Long-run dP/dG = 6.0
options_template.feedback: Correct. Short-run: (1.0 * 3.0) / [1 - (-0.5)(1.0)] = 3.0 / 1.5 = 2.0. Long-run: -3.0 / (-0.5) = 6.0. Prices rise more in the long run because all demand pressure is absorbed into P once Y returns to Y*.

options_template.text: Short-run dP/dG = 6.0; Long-run dP/dG = 2.0
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Short-Run vs. Long-Run Swap): The long-run price impact (6.0) exceeds the short-run impact (2.0) because SRAS shifts leftward during self-correction.

options_template.text: Short-run dP/dG = 3.0; Long-run dP/dG = 6.0
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted Denominator): Setting short-run dP/dG = S_Y * D_G = 3.0 omits the denominator 1 - D_P * S_Y = 1.5.

options_template.text: Short-run dP/dG = 2.0; Long-run dP/dG = 0.0
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Confusing Long-Run Output with Long-Run Price): In the long run, dY/dG approaches 0, whereas dP/dG approaches -D_G / D_P = 6.0 > 0.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Why Adverse Supply Shocks Create a Policy Dilemma
questions.prompt_template: Why does an adverse Short-Run Aggregate Supply (SRAS) shock create a severe macroeconomic policy dilemma for central banks and fiscal authorities that a negative Aggregate Demand (AD) shock does not?

hints.text: Compare the directions of ΔY and ΔP under a negative AD shock versus an adverse SRAS shock.
Remember that standard fiscal and monetary tools primarily shift AD, which moves Y and P in the same direction.

options_template.text: Because demand-management tools can only shift AD: in stagflation, stimulating AD reduces unemployment at the cost of worsening inflation, whereas tightening AD curbs inflation at the cost of deepening the recession.
options_template.feedback: Correct. A negative AD shock lowers both Y and P (so expansionary AD policy fixes both problems simultaneously), whereas an adverse SRAS shock lowers Y while raising P, forcing a painful trade-off.

options_template.text: Because fiscal and monetary policies have no effect on Aggregate Demand during a supply shock.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Policy Impotence Myth): Fiscal and monetary policies still shift AD during a supply shock; the dilemma is that shifting AD improves one goal (output or inflation) only by worsening the other.

options_template.text: Because an adverse supply shock shifts LRAS rightward, making stabilization unnecessary.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Confusing Adverse Cost Shock with Productivity Boom): An adverse energy or input shock shifts SRAS leftward, creating both higher unemployment and higher inflation.

options_template.text: Because a negative AD shock raises inflation while lowering output, leaving policymakers with no viable tool.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Shock-Symptom Swap): A negative AD shock lowers both Y and P; it is an adverse SRAS shock that raises P while lowering Y.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Identifying the 2008-2009 Shock from FRED Co-Movements
questions.prompt_template: During the 2008-2009 Great Recession, U.S. FRED data showed Real GDP (GDPC1) contracting, headline consumer prices (CPIAUCSL) decelerating/dipping, and the unemployment rate (UNRATE) surging toward 10%. Which AD-AS diagnosis matches this empirical signature?

hints.text: Check whether GDPC1 (output) and CPIAUCSL (prices) moved in the same direction or opposite directions.
Same-direction downward movement of Y and P points to a leftward shift of AD.

options_template.text: An adverse supply shock (stagflation) shifting SRAS leftward.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Stagflation Misdiagnosis): An adverse supply shock would push CPIAUCSL sharply upward alongside falling GDPC1, whereas 2008-2009 saw disinflation/dipping prices.

options_template.text: A severe adverse demand shock shifting AD leftward.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Falling real output (GDPC1), rising unemployment (UNRATE), and decelerating/falling prices (CPIAUCSL) represent same-direction movement of Y and P—the classic signature of a leftward AD shift.

options_template.text: A favorable productivity shock shifting SRAS and LRAS rightward.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Favorable Supply Misdiagnosis): A favorable supply shock lowers prices while raising GDPC1 and lowering UNRATE, contradicting the 2008-2009 contraction.

options_template.text: A positive demand shock creating an inflationary gap.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Expansion Misdiagnosis): A positive demand shock raises GDPC1 and CPIAUCSL while lowering UNRATE.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Identifying the 1973-1975 and 1979-1980 Oil Shocks
questions.prompt_template: During the 1973-1975 and 1979-1980 oil price shocks, FRED series recorded falling Real GDP (GDPC1) and jumping unemployment (UNRATE) at the same time CPIAUCSL inflation exceeded 11%. What is the unmistakable AD-AS interpretation of these episodes?

hints.text: Notice that real output (GDPC1) fell while consumer price inflation (CPIAUCSL) surged above 11%.
Opposite-direction movement of Y and P identifies a supply shock rather than a demand shock.

options_template.text: Pure positive demand shocks caused by excessive consumer optimism.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Demand-Expansion Misdiagnosis): Positive demand shocks raise GDPC1 and lower UNRATE alongside rising inflation.

options_template.text: Pure negative demand shocks caused by tight monetary policy alone.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Demand-Contraction Misdiagnosis): A negative demand shock lowers inflation rather than pushing CPIAUCSL above 11%.

options_template.text: Adverse supply shocks (stagflation) shifting SRAS leftward as energy input costs spiked.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Opposite-direction movement—falling GDPC1 and rising UNRATE alongside double-digit CPIAUCSL inflation—is the empirical footprint of a leftward SRAS shift.

options_template.text: Movement along a stationary AD curve driven by lower interest rates.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Movement-Along-Curve Misdiagnosis): Moving down along AD raises output and lowers P; stagflation requires shifting SRAS leftward.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Decomposing the 2021-2023 Combined Shock
questions.prompt_template: How does the AD-AS model resolve the 2021-2023 U.S. inflation puzzle in which CPIAUCSL inflation surged above 9% even as unemployment fell toward 3.4% and real GDP recovery moderated?

hints.text: Recall the 'Bring It Home' closing anchor: what two forces collided in 2021-2022?
Combine a rightward AD shift with a leftward SRAS shift and check the net effect on P and Y.

options_template.text: It reflects a single negative demand shock that lowered both output and inflation.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Contradicted by Data): CPIAUCSL rose above 9% and UNRATE fell toward 3.4%, the opposite of a negative demand shock.

options_template.text: It reflects a pure favorable supply shock that lowered production costs across global supply chains.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inverted Supply Conditions): 2021-2022 featured semiconductor shortages, port bottlenecks, and energy price spikes—adverse, not favorable, supply conditions.

options_template.text: It reflects simultaneous positive demand shocks (fiscal stimulus and pent-up spending shifting AD right) and adverse supply shocks (bottlenecks and energy spikes shifting SRAS left), which both pushed P sharply upward.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Rightward AD and leftward SRAS reinforced each other to drive inflation above 9%, while pulling real output in opposite directions so unemployment stayed low even as GDP growth moderated.

options_template.text: It shows that the AD-AS model cannot analyze episodes where both fiscal policy and energy prices change.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Model Dismissal): Comparative statics with simultaneous AD and SRAS shifts is a core analytical strength of the AD-AS framework.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Evaluating the 2022-2024 Fed Rate-Hike Transmission
questions.prompt_template: During 2022-2023, the Federal Reserve raised its administered interest-rate corridor, pushing 30-year fixed mortgage rates from roughly 3% to over 7%. Why did this shift the U.S. AD curve leftward even before overall consumer prices declined?

hints.text: Think about how a jump in 30-year mortgage rates from ~3% to >7% affects housing construction (I) and auto/durable purchases (C).
Ask whether this spending reduction occurred because P changed or because borrowing costs rose at every given P.

options_template.text: Because higher policy and mortgage rates directly reduced planned residential investment (I) and interest-sensitive durable consumption (C) at every aggregate price level.
options_template.feedback: Correct. A discretionary tightening of policy interest rates raises borrowing costs independently of P, curtailing planned housing investment and durable purchases and shifting AD leftward to cool excess demand.

options_template.text: Because higher mortgage rates reduced the nominal money supply directly through household wealth destruction.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Channel Misattribution): The primary direct mechanism cited is higher borrowing costs curtailing residential investment (I) and durable consumption (C).

options_template.text: Because higher interest rates immediately shifted LRAS rightward, eliminating inflation without affecting AD.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Supply-Side Misattribution): Higher interest rates discourage capital investment rather than immediately expanding long-run productive capacity.

options_template.text: Because higher mortgage rates caused a downward movement along the existing AD curve.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Movement vs. Shift Error): A movement along AD is caused by a change in the aggregate price level P, whereas a Fed rate hike shifts the AD curve itself.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: AI Infrastructure: Short Run vs. Long Run
questions.title: Macroeconomic Dynamics of AI Capital Investment
questions.prompt_template: Heavy private investment in AI data centers, automation, and cloud computing affects the macroeconomy across two horizons. Which AD-AS comparison accurately contrasts its initial short-run impact with its potential multi-year productivity impact?

hints.text: Separate the immediate spending effect (business investment I in AD) from the later productivity effect (output per worker in SRAS/LRAS).
Remember that higher productivity lowers unit labor costs and expands potential GDP Y*.

options_template.text: Initially, higher business investment (I) shifts AD rightward (raising Y and P); over a multi-year horizon, if AI raises output per worker, lower unit labor costs shift both SRAS and LRAS rightward for higher non-inflationary potential output (Y*).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Capital spending first stimulates Aggregate Demand via I, whereas realized economy-wide productivity gains subsequently reduce unit costs and expand sustainable capacity Y*.

options_template.text: Initially, business investment shifts LRAS leftward; over the long run, it shifts AD leftward.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inverted Investment Effects): Business investment adds to AD immediately and builds capital/productivity that expands—rather than shrinks—LRAS.

options_template.text: AI investment shifts only AD permanently and can never affect SRAS or LRAS.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Demand-Only View): If automation and cloud technologies raise output per worker across sectors, they directly lower unit costs (SRAS) and raise potential output (LRAS).

options_template.text: AI investment immediately lowers the price level in the short run and permanently reduces Y* in the long run.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Reversed Price and Output Effects): An investment boom puts upward demand pressure on P initially and, if productivity-enhancing, raises Y* over time.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Why Policymakers Rarely Wait for Recessionary Self-Correction
questions.prompt_template: In theory, an economy in a deep recessionary gap (Y < Y*) can self-correct without policy intervention as falling nominal wages shift SRAS rightward. Why do policymakers frequently favor active expansionary policy instead of waiting for self-correction?

hints.text: Think about how quickly workers and firms accept cuts in nominal wages during a recession.
Compare the speed and unemployment cost of waiting for wages to fall versus shifting AD back toward Y*.

options_template.text: Because nominal wages are sticky downward (due to contracts and worker resistance), making unassisted self-correction from recessions slow and socially costly in prolonged high unemployment.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Downward nominal wage rigidity delays the rightward shift of SRAS, meaning relying solely on self-correction can leave unemployment painfully above u* for years.

options_template.text: Because SRAS can never shift rightward under any economic conditions.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Absolute Impossibility Claim): SRAS can shift rightward when input costs or wage growth fall, but downward nominal wage stickiness makes the process sluggish.

options_template.text: Because expansionary AD policy permanently shifts LRAS to the right even without productivity growth.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Demand-Driven LRAS Myth): Expansionary AD policy closes a recessionary gap back to existing Y*; it does not conjure permanent LRAS growth out of thin air.

options_template.text: Because self-correction from a recessionary gap causes hyperinflation.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inverted Price Direction): Self-correction from a recessionary gap shifts SRAS rightward, which puts downward—not upward—pressure on the price level.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Fiscal Stimulus in an Inflationary Gap
questions.title: Long-Run Consequence of Stimulating an Overheated Economy
questions.prompt_template: Suppose an economy is already operating at or above potential output (Y >= Y*). If lawmakers enact a large, permanent increase in government spending (G) financed by borrowing, what does the AD-AS framework predict in the long run?

hints.text: Apply the long-run comparative-statics result: along vertical LRAS, lim (S_Y -> inf) dY/dG = 0 while dP/dG > 0.
Trace AD shifting right from Y* and then trace the wage adjustment that brings Y back to Y*.

options_template.text: Real GDP remains permanently above Y* while the aggregate price level stays unchanged.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ignoring Long-Run Vertical LRAS): Because LRAS is vertical at Y*, pure demand stimulus cannot sustain real output permanently above potential.

options_template.text: Short-run output expands further above Y*, but tight labor markets bid up nominal wages and shift SRAS leftward until output returns to Y* at a permanently higher price level.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Stimulating AD when the economy is already at or above Y* generates temporary overheating followed by wage-driven SRAS contraction, leaving long-run Y unchanged at Y* and P permanently higher.

options_template.text: Both real GDP and the aggregate price level fall permanently below their initial levels.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Reversed Fiscal Direction): Higher G shifts AD rightward, raising—not lowering—P in both the short run and long run.

options_template.text: SRAS automatically shifts rightward to match the higher AD so inflation never rises.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inverted Self-Correction): Tight labor markets raise nominal wages and shift SRAS leftward, not rightward.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Why Upward-Sloping SRAS Dampens the Output Multiplier
questions.prompt_template: In the comparative-statics extension dY/dG = D_G / (1 - D_P * S_Y), why is the short-run fiscal output multiplier strictly smaller in the AD-SRAS model (S_Y > 0) than in the fixed-price Keynesian Cross (S_Y = 0)?

hints.text: Examine the signs of D_P (< 0) and S_Y (> 0) in the denominator 1 - D_P * S_Y.
Ask what happens to C, I, and NX when rising P triggers the wealth, interest-rate, and exchange-rate effects in reverse.

options_template.text: Because when AD shifts right along an upward-sloping SRAS curve, the resulting rise in P crowds out price-sensitive spending via the wealth, interest-rate, and exchange-rate channels (making 1 - D_P * S_Y > 1).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Since D_P < 0 and S_Y > 0, the denominator 1 - D_P * S_Y exceeds 1, reflecting that higher prices reduce real wealth, raise interest rates, and reduce net exports—partially offsetting the initial fiscal boost.

options_template.text: Because higher government spending reduces the marginal propensity to consume to zero.
