options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (MPC Misattribution): The dampening arises from endogenous price-level increases (S_Y > 0 and D_P < 0), not from a collapse in the MPC.

options_template.text: Because in the AD-SRAS model, D_P > 0 and S_Y < 0, which makes the denominator negative.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inverted Curve Slopes): AD slopes downward (D_P < 0) and SRAS slopes upward (S_Y > 0), so -D_P * S_Y is positive and 1 - D_P * S_Y > 1.

options_template.text: Because the Keynesian Cross includes net exports while the AD-SRAS model excludes them.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Expenditure Scope Myth): Both frameworks include all components of aggregate expenditure; the difference is fixed P (S_Y = 0) versus flexible P along upward-sloping SRAS (S_Y > 0).

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Why Aggregate Co-Movement Alone Cannot Prove Causality
questions.prompt_template: Why can observing raw co-movement between quarterly Real GDP (GDPC1) and monthly CPI (CPIAUCSL) alone NOT definitively prove the causal magnitude of a demand shock versus a supply shock?

hints.text: Recall the Chapter 9 Check Your Understanding #6 and FRED Data Diagnostics caveat.
Consider what happens when both AD and SRAS shift at the same time (as in 2021-2023) and when one series is quarterly while the other is monthly.

options_template.text: Because GDPC1 and CPIAUCSL are mathematically identical series.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Series Conflation): GDPC1 measures real output quantities, whereas CPIAUCSL measures consumer prices.

options_template.text: Because simultaneous demand and supply shocks can offset or reinforce each other, and quarterly-versus-monthly frequency mismatches plus statistical revisions obscure timing—requiring structural identification and relative input-price evidence.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Observational co-movement conflates overlapping shocks and timing/revision noise; economists must examine relative input prices (e.g., energy, wages) and structural identification strategies to separate demand from supply.

options_template.text: Because FRED data never reflect business cycle fluctuations.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Data Dismissal): FRED series clearly capture recessions and inflation spikes, but raw two-variable correlation does not isolate overlapping structural shocks.

options_template.text: Because AD shocks and SRAS shocks always produce identical co-movements in GDPC1 and CPIAUCSL.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Overstating Ambiguity): Pure AD shocks produce positive co-movement while pure SRAS shocks produce negative co-movement; the identification problem arises when shocks overlap or frequencies/revisions blur timing.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Unanchored Inflation Expectations in AD-AS
questions.prompt_template: Suppose no new energy shock occurs and Aggregate Demand stops growing, yet households and workers lose confidence in price stability and revise their expected price level (P^e) sharply upward. What does the AD-AS model predict?

hints.text: Trace how higher P^e enters nominal wage negotiations and the SRAS equation P = P^e + (1/gamma)(Y - Y*).
When SRAS shifts leftward against a stationary AD curve, check the resulting changes in P and Y.

options_template.text: Nothing happens because only actual energy prices can shift SRAS.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ignoring Expectations Channel): Expected price level P^e is a direct shifter of SRAS through nominal wage bargaining.

options_template.text: Workers demand higher nominal wages to protect real purchasing power, shifting SRAS leftward and generating self-fulfilling stagflation (higher P and lower Y).
options_template.feedback: Correct. When P^e rises, wage contracts build in higher nominal labor costs today, shifting SRAS leftward along AD and pushing actual inflation up even as real output contracts.

options_template.text: Higher expected inflation shifts LRAS rightward because workers supply more labor.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Nominal Expectations vs. Real Capacity): Higher expected inflation is a nominal distortion that shifts SRAS leftward, not a real expansion of LRAS.

options_template.text: SRAS shifts rightward, automatically eliminating inflation without any loss of output.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Reversed SRAS Direction): Rising P^e raises nominal wage demands and unit costs, shifting SRAS leftward, not rightward.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Achieving Sustainable Non-Inflationary GDP Growth
questions.prompt_template: A country wants to raise its real GDP permanently over the next decade without generating persistent upward pressure on the aggregate price level. According to the AD-AS framework, which policy strategy can achieve this goal?

hints.text: Ask which curve must shift rightward to allow permanently higher real GDP without persistent inflation.
Distinguish policies that shift AD from policies that expand potential output Y* (LRAS).

options_template.text: Repeatedly cutting policy interest rates to shift AD rightward every year while leaving LRAS fixed.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inflationary Demand-Only Growth): Repeatedly shifting AD against a fixed vertical LRAS produces ongoing inflation without raising long-run potential output Y*.

options_template.text: Repeatedly increasing government transfer payments to boost household consumption while ignoring capital formation.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Short-Run Demand Focus): Pure consumption stimulus shifts AD rightward but does not expand the economy's long-run productive capacity Y*.

options_template.text: Investing in human capital, physical infrastructure, and technological innovation that raises total factor productivity, shifting both SRAS and vertical LRAS rightward.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Expanding real productive capacity shifts LRAS and SRAS rightward, increasing sustainable potential output Y* while easing unit cost and price-level pressures.

options_template.text: Legislating higher nominal wages across all industries to increase worker purchasing power.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Cost-Push Confusion): Higher nominal wages without matching productivity gains raise unit labor costs and shift SRAS leftward, causing higher prices and lower output.
